item.title: Inside the lavish lifestyle of ultra-wealthy Dem endorsed by top Bernie Sanders group
item.description: Eric Jones reports up to $86 million in assets and an $8 million salary while campaigning against corporate influence in California's 4th district race.
item.content:encoded:
A Democratic House nominee in California, who has made affordability a key issue in his campaign and is backed by a top Bernie Sanders group, is worth up to tens of millions of dollars.

Eric Jones, who is running in California’s 4th Congressional District, reported between $18 and $86 million in assets, according to campaign finance disclosures.

Along with other holdings, Jones owns a $4.6 million Napa home, which includes a pool, with furnishings and artwork estimated at between $393,000 to $578,000, a Fox News Digital review found.

His evaluation contrasts sharply with his populist campaign platform, where he has painted himself as a relatable figure who has also grappled with concerns about affordability.

TOP DEM HOPEFUL FLIPS SCRIPT AFTER YEARS IN SOCIALIST ORBIT WITH PUZZLING CLAIM

"The cost of living continues to rise," Jones said in an April campaign video.

"I’m running for Congress because I know what it feels like to do everything right and still struggle… I will never take a dollar from a corporate PAC, I will never take a dime from a lobbyist, and I will never trade a stock while I serve you in Congress."

Throughout his campaign, Jones has highlighted his family’s struggle with financial stability. He grew up in a military family and had a disabled father. According to Jones, the family also struggled to overcome medical debt, relying on Medicaid and food stamps.

On his website, Jones has listed three main priorities: ending corruption, lowering the cost of living and resource sustainability in government. His stances have attracted endorsements from progressive groups like Indivisible and Our Revolution, organizations with ties to progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who has repeatedly attacked millionaires and billionaires throughout his career despite being a millionaire himself.

"A Congress of millionaires will legislate for their corporate investments. A Congress from the working class will legislate for the people," Our Revolution posted on X in 2022.

In a 2025 post, Our Revolution shared a graphic attacking the number of millionaires in Congress. Despite several posts against millionaires and the wealthy, the group gave him a glowing endorsement.

"Our Revolution believes in leaders who fight for working people with integrity and courage," the endorsement said. "Eric Jones is one of those leaders — and we’re proud to stand with him as he brings a people-powered movement to Congress in 2026."

Jones’ wealth came from his career in investing. Shortly after graduating from Yale, he joined Dragoneer Investment Group in San Francisco in 2013. The group is a venture capital group that invests in technology and high-growth companies like ByteDance and Alibaba, a pair of Chinese businesses with deep ties to the Chinese Communist Party.

By the age of 27 in 2017, Jones had become the group’s first non-founding partner. During his 12 years with the group, Dragoneer exploded in value, going from managing $180 million in assets to $24 billion.

'SQUAD' DEM DISMISSES FRAUD PROBE SPECULATION AFTER $29M NET-WORTH DROP

Jones listed an $8 million salary with the group from last year in his campaign financial disclosure.

The extravagances of his roughly 3,000-square-foot home were featured by Architectural Digest in a June 9 home tour as part of a profile piece on his wife, who works for an architecture firm as a designer.

Among his many assets, Jones’ furnishing collection includes a wall-hung ceramic sculpture worth up to $60,000, a "Polly chair" estimated at somewhere between $10,000 and $25,000 and a column coffee table worth $6,000. 

Now, as a candidate, Jones has campaigned against corporate influence in politics and a system that he argues is rigged in favor of larger corporations. He has identified that kind of structure as a key part of his plan to address affordability.

"Rent, groceries, utilities, health care, childcare — everything costs more while giant corporations post record profits and pay little or nothing in taxes," Jones states on his website.

"That’s not an accident. It’s a system rigged to work for the people at the top."

DEM CIVIL WAR HITS PRIMARY DEBATE STAGE IN FIERY BATTLEGROUND SHOWDOWN: 'WHAT ARE YOU HIDING?'

When approached about his personal wealth, Jones said he doesn't believe his personal wealth clashes with a message of affordability.

"I grew up poor in rural America with a veteran father fighting medical debt and opioid addiction. I built businesses, created jobs and achieved the American Dream – I'm lucky that this country gave me that opportunity, and I'll never forget where I came from. We should have leaders who've built something and know what medical debt feels like, not career politicians who've gotten rich serving Big Pharma and the insurance lobby. Every family in this district deserves that same shot at the American Dream, that's why I'm running," Jones said in a statement.

Having placed in the top two candidates in the primary, Jones will face off against incumbent Rep. Mike Thompson, D-Calif., in the state’s Nov. 3 general election.

item.title: Jack Smith's Senate phone records probe turns to Verizon's handling of subpoenas
item.description: Sen. Chuck Grassley and 15 senators demand Verizon explain why it failed to disclose Jack Smith's Arctic Frost subpoena for congressional phone records.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: The Senate investigation into former Special Counsel Jack Smith's "Arctic Frost" probe is widening, as Republican lawmakers question Verizon’s handling of subpoenas for senators’ phone records after the telecom giant failed to disclose one during an earlier congressional records search.

As part of Operation Arctic Frost — the codename for the FBI's Trump-election-interference probe with Smith placed at the helm — prosecutors subpoenaed Verizon and other phone carriers for toll records tied to members of Congress and other Republican figures. Several conservative entities were swept up in the probe, including the late Charlie Kirk.

Verizon later acknowledged omitting Smith's subpoena from its congressional record search.

The dispute centers less on Verizon's compliance with the subpoena than on what the company knew afterward, whether it should have notified Congress and why it failed to disclose the subpoena during an earlier records search.

BIDEN SPECIAL COUNSEL’S 'RUNAWAY TRAIN’ SCOOPED UP SENSITIVE LAWMAKER INFO: 'ABUSE OF POWER'

Smith’s investigation has faced increased scrutiny in recent months, and now Senate Judiciary Chairman Charles Grassley, R-Iowa — whose records were among those obtained — and a slew of his colleagues want to know what Verizon knew, when it knew it and whether the company should have notified affected members of Congress after turning over their phone records to Smith's team.

"Jack Smith oversaw a sweeping and unprecedented investigation that swept-up records from hundreds of Republican entities, including the phone toll records and text messages from myself and dozens of my colleagues," Grassley told Fox News Digital Friday.

Toll records are essentially the metadata of a telephone call — and exclude the contents of the conversation. They often include the phone numbers involved, date, time, duration and often the operative cell-tower location.

MAJOR PHONE CARRIERS REVEAL JACK SMITH’S SUBPOENAS FOR REPUBLICAN SENATORS’ RECORDS

"Congress deserves to know the full picture of how Smith carried out Arctic Frost so it never happens again."

"As part of our investigation, we need to fully understand what Verizon knew about Smith’s subpoenas, when they became aware members were impacted and why the company didn’t inform members like they were supposed to," he said.

In a Thursday letter to Verizon CEO Daniel Schulman, Grassley, Senate Investigations Subcommittee chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., and more than a dozen senators said they remain concerned not only by the alleged "abuse of power by federal government actors… but also with Verizon’s disclosures of (m)embers’ phone records pursuant to a May 25, 2023, subpoena (and) its failure to disclose this information to affected Members."

JACK SMITH THRUST BACK INTO SPOTLIGHT AT BLANCHE HEARING OVER EXPOSED SENATORS’ MESSAGES'

Of the signatories, Sens. Bill Hagerty IV and Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., Rick Scott, R-Fla., Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., Mike Lee, R-Utah, Ted Cruz, R-Texas, Josh Hawley, R-Mo., John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., also had their phone toll records or text messages swept up by Smith.

Their inquiry noted he asked Verizon in October 2023 to identify Justice Department or other federal law enforcement requests involving Senate devices used by his staff dating back to 2016.

The senator wrote that the subpoena was not disclosed in Verizon's initial response, and Grassley said Congress did not learn of it until Verizon acknowledged in 2025 that "human error" had caused its omission.

In its original October 2023 response to Grassley, Verizon wrote that it often limits retention of legal processes received to a period of four years, and attested it had no records to produce prior to October 2019.

"This raises questions as to whether Verizon discovered legal process from DOJ for Senate devices and lines, including the May 2023 Arctic Frost subpoena, in its search from October 1, 2019, to October 27, 2023, for responsive records to Chairman Grassley’s request," Grassley wrote in his new letter.

Therefore, Grassley and 15 other senators are demanding Verizon brass explain when they first learned Smith’s subpoena sought phone records that included members of Congress and when they discovered it had provided "tolling data" connected to those members and transmitted it to Smith.

Fox News Digital reached out to Verizon for comment.

Grassley’s new letter suggests the October 2023 exchange may be the key to determining whether Verizon merely missed the subpoena or discovered it and failed to disclose it.

"On what date were Daniel Schulman, Vandana Venkatesh, Hans Vestberg, and Craig Silliman first informed about the May 25, 2023, subpoena?" they asked of Verizon’s front office.

The senators also asked that Verizon explain its "human error" revelation in more specificity and produce internal records from May 2023 to October 2025 that discuss whether the company believed it was obligated to notify the implicated members of Congress or the Senate Sergeant-at-Arms (SAA).

The "human error" explanation also left unanswered why Smith’s May 25, 2023, "Arctic Frost" subpoena was omitted from Verizon's review of legal process involving SAA phone lines, even though the company acknowledged that two SAA numbers were included in the subpoena.

In 2025, documents provided to Grassley revealed Verizon complied with Smith while AT&T resisted the requests.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

However, both subpoenas were accompanied by gag orders signed by Obama-appointed District of Columbia federal Judge James Boasberg, a frequent foil of President Donald Trump’s. Boasberg directed Verizon and AT&T not to disclose the subpoenas to lawmakers for a period of one year.

The DOJ has issued subpoenas for lawmakers' information in the past, but former inspector general Michael Horowitz cautioned against it except in limited circumstances in a report published in 2025, saying that doing so "risks chilling Congress’s ability to conduct oversight of the executive branch."

Grassley’s letter gives Verizon until Aug. 13 to explain when it knew senators’ records were involved, who inside the company was informed and why the May 2023 subpoena did not surface in its earlier response to Congress.

Senate Judiciary Committee Republicans have branded Smith's "Arctic Frost" as "worse than Watergate."

Fox News Digital reached out to counsel for Smith for comment.

item.title: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson names Andre Sayles as interim police chief after Barnes resignation
item.description: Deputy Chief Andre Sayles takes over as interim Seattle police chief after Shon Barnes' resignation following the deadly Bite of Seattle shooting.
item.content:encoded:
Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson announced a new interim police chief on Friday following the resignation of Police Chief Shon Barnes after a deadly shooting at a food festival over the weekend.

"I do not take lightly what it means to make decisions that affect people's safety and their lives," Wilson said in a Friday morning news conference before announcing she had selected Deputy Chief Andre Sayles as interim police chief.

She added, "I chose Andre Sayles because he has done this job before and can hit the ground running. He served as chief of police in Wisconsin, where he led with a community-focused approach that strengthened both public safety and community trust. He has earned the respect of our police force in his time here, and that is exactly what we need right now."

SEATTLE POLICE CHIEF SNAPS OVER CHICAGO HOME QUESTIONS, ABSENCE FROM CITY AFTER MASS SHOOTING

Barnes had come under criticism after two people died and four others were shot at the Bite of Seattle food festival at Seattle Center on Sunday.

Barnes described the shooting a "targeted" and "gang-related" but said the victims were "not related to the suspects in any way."

One arrest has been made, and one person believed to have been involved in the shooting has died.

THIRD SUSPECT EMERGES IN DEADLY SEATTLE MASS SHOOTING, ONE ALLEGED GUNMAN FOUND DEAD

Sayles said on Friday that the department is continuing to investigate and looking for any other possible suspects involved in the shooting.

Barnes resigned on Thursday, saying in a statement through his attorney that Wilson had requested his resignation on Wednesday, and he "believes this is the best path forward for the city, which is still reeling from the shock and pain caused by the tragic events at the Seattle Center."

In an earlier statement, Wilson said: "Chief Barnes has served this department and this city with dedication, and I am grateful for his service. The courage and professionalism that the officers of the Seattle Police Department showed deserves to be honored."

GUNFIRE ERUPTS NEAR SEATTLE MAYOR’S EVENT AS FAMILIES, CHILDREN GATHER

She added, "I share Chief Barnes' hope that we can return our focus to addressing youth gun violence and ensuring that every family can feel safe in their neighborhood and across the city."

Sayles acknowledged that this week has been "difficult, but I also know what this department and city are capable of. When we come together with a common goal of keeping our community safe."

He committed to uniting a department "grounded in service, pride and dedication."

"The ongoing investigation into the Seattle Center shooting remains a top priority," he added. "The men and women of the department continue working tirelessly to identify and arrest anyone responsible. In light of the tragic incident, the Seattle Police Department has heard from our community about safety concerns at public gatherings and events."

Sayles said the department will be increasing staff at all remaining major summer events.

Wilson added that she is also searching for Barnes’ permanent replacement as police chief, saying it "will focus on someone who drives operational excellence and leads organizational change."

She said the "people of Seattle deserve a voice in this selection," explaining that a search committee will be formed that is representative of different communities in the city.

"I will be looking for someone who can be an effective leader of our police department, from top to bottom," she said. "In particular, that means listening to and building relationships with the people standing behind me, the experienced and dedicated people who are leading our officers on the ground in neighborhoods across our city every single day."

Wilson added that she was also looking for someone who could earn the respect of the police force, "while also leading needed changes to culture and protocol in a way that is firm and fair. I will be looking for someone who can practice clear communication in stressful situations."

item.title: Paulina Gretzky celebrates rumored LIV deal in a watermelon dress, Monica McNutt embarrasses ESPN & Paige!
item.description: Monica McNutt delivered her ESPN takes from a nail salon while Karl Ravech quietly returned to work after being laid off just weeks earlier.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday–Friday on OutKick.com.

Final Friday of July ... Final DAY of July.

Has this been the longest month ever? I feel like we get two months every year that seemingly last forever.

January and July.

The rest fly by. But those? They just drag. I don't mind July dragging a bit because we respect summer around here (until Labor Day Monday), but January is always such a grind.

Luckily, that's not a today problem. There are no problems today. We're on the brink of August, which is the true calm before the storm.

Let's ride this out together and end the month strong.

Welcome to a Friday Nightcaps — the one where Paulina Gretzky celebrates the rumored LIV deal on a yacht in a watermelon dress. As one does, of course.

What else? I've got Tony Romo getting put on leave (any guesses on when he'll be back?!), insufferable ESPN analyst Monica McNutt somehow becoming even more insufferable, and would you ever go back to a job that fired you just for the love of the game?

Karl Ravech did it last night, and I couldn't believe my eyes. What a move.

Pro's pro.

Grab you whatever you need to get you through the rest of this day — dealer's choice! — and settle in for a Friday 'Cap!

Let's spin the wheel and start with ... OutKick fan-favorite, Monica McNutt! You didn't think we'd go a whole day without talking about the WNBA, did you?

To be fair, we're not really going to talk about it today. Don't worry. Don't leave! I promise, this has nothing to do with that shameful league.

Instead, it has to do with McNutt, ESPN's WNBA analyst, who is pretty much hated by everyone. Somehow, she still has a job after all the layoffs earlier this month (more on them in a bit), which means we'll get plenty of racial Caitlin Clark takes over the next month or two.

Thank goodness.

Anyway, McNutt joined a version of SportsCenter that nobody watches last night, and decided to give her hot take(s) from a nail salon, which was, frankly, the most pathetic thing I've seen from that network in a while.

Imagine this coming on your screen and not changing the channel:

Lordy. What a time to be alive. What a world we live in at the moment. This isn't the first time we've heard from McNutt this week, by the way.

Don't forget, just a few days ago, she stuffed Caitlin Clark in a locker and insisted she was to blame for the negative headlines surrounding the WNBA because she lacks "accountability" and "self-awareness."

Seriously:

Goodness gracious. And Ryan Clark had the audacity to blame racism on his firing when Monica McNutt is still employed and allowed to spout off takes like that.

Yeah, OK, Rhino! Whatever you say.

Anyway, who else is looking forward to another drama-free weekend out of the WNBA!? Sophie Cunningham plays tonight in lefty Portland. Surely nothing will happen.

OK, moving on ...

... From one ESPN staffer to another (former?) ESPN staffer:

Whoaaaaaaaa Nellie! Imagine my surprise last night when I flipped to the Nats-Braves game, and heard Karl Ravech on the call.

Yes, the same Karl Ravech that was part of those layoffs a few weeks ago. He's back! He just showed back up to work like nothing happened.

No explanation. No comment. No nothin'. Just put his hard-hat on and acted like he never left. Amazing.

Some context:

Should tell you everything you need to know.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON’T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

OK, let's rapid-fire this Friday class into a big Friday night. First up? Amazingly, LIV Gold reportedly has an interested investor who is willing to step in and essentially save the league. Nothing is official, but that's the word on the street right now.

Paulina Gretzky — wife of Dustin Johnson — seems to be celebrating the news appropriately:

Welcome back to class, Paulina! Been a while. Remember when Dustin Johnson used to be good at golf and actually in contention? Seems like a lifetime ago.

DJ, by the way, is coming off a literal no-show at the British Open earlier this month. He skipped his last qualifier, and decided to start vacation a few weeks early.

Paulina Gretzky returns to the Masters Par 3 Contest caddying for Dustin Johnson

Seems like Paulina approves.

Next? Let's check in with Tony Romo on the heels of last weekend's OWI arrest:

On leave "indefinitely." Yeah, OK. Hogwash! Quick, who wants to guess when this "leave" gets lifted?

IIIIIIIIIIIIII don't know, Jiiiiiiiiiim!

Sure you do! Sept. 4 — one day before the NFL season kicks off. CBS has said that JJ Watt will replace Romo alongside Nantz, but I'll believe that when I see it.

There's a Packers-Vikings 4:25 game calling his name that Sunday.

OK, that's it for today — and this week. Good week. Great month. Time to turn the page and really start to crank things up.

Here's Paige Spiranac promoting some new golf #content to take us into August.

See you Monday.

item.title: Caitlin Clark, Indiana Fever are undervalued against the slumping Portland Fire on ‘Sophie Night’
item.description: Indiana Fever are costly -7.5 favorites over Portland Fire, but key injury tags on Caitlin Clark and Aliyah Boston make the spread intriguing.
item.content:encoded:
While my colleagues will be locked into what’s going on outside the arena, I’ll be sweating my betting action in the Indiana Fever (18-10) at Portland Fire (11-17) Friday at the Moda Center at 10:00 p.m. ET.

Reportedly, there will be "protect women in sports" activists, and probably LGBTQ+ activists, rallying in support, or opposition, of Indiana backup SG Sophie Cunningham’s recent comments like "young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men".

SHOULD NBA COMMISSIONER ADAM SILVER STEP IN OVER THE WNBA'S HANDLING OF THE SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SITUATION?

Again, I’m not here to discuss this hot-button issue. Frankly, I’m motivated by self-interest, which includes getting page views for this article by name-dropping Caitlin Clark and mentioning the drama, and more importantly, cashing my Fever-Fire bet.

That said, Indiana is an expensive -7.5 (-120) favorite and -325 on the moneyline at DraftKings, and the total for this game is 187.5. Without further ado, let’s discuss the stuff that really matters. At least to me.

These teams split the first two meetings this season with the home team winning and covering both. The Fever have won eight of their last 10 games, including four straight. Portland, on the other hand, is just 3-7 over its past 10 games and has lost three in a row.

There are "probable" tags on two key players for Indiana on its injury report: Clark and C Aliyah Boston. Clark leads the Fever in assists per game and is their highest usage player. Boston is their third-leading scorer and leading rebounder. The Fire are missing sharpshooting SG Sarah Ashlee Barker.

Even though Clark and Boston are expected to play Friday, this line hints at their possible absence. Indiana was an -11.5 favorite in Portland earlier this season with Clark and Boston available.

CAITLIN CLARK MAKES WNBA HISTORY WITH RECORD-BREAKING GAME AFTER WEEKS OF CONTROVERSY

Coincidentally, or maybe not, Clark played in Indy’s 100-84 loss to Portland and missed the Fever’s 90-73 blowout win over the Fire. She had her worst game of the season vs. the Fire, scoring just 6 points on 1-for-7 shooting in a season-low 21:45 minutes.

Yet, Barker’s absence is bigger than the market is accounting for. Especially since the Fire have the third-highest 3-point attempt rate in the WNBA. Barker has the second-highest on/off net rating on the team at +7.0 while shooting 50.2% from the field and 40.0% from behind the arc.

Also, because of Clark’s popularity, Indiana All-Star guard Kelsey Mitchell is underrated or overlooked. Mitchell averages a team-best 23.5 points per game. If Clark or Boston gets scratched Friday, Mitchell’s usage should increase and that ain’t a bad thing.

Finally, the "battle for possessions" is the most important thing in professional basketball and the Fever has a better rebounding rate on both ends of the floor. In fact, Portland has the worst defensive rebounding rate in the WNBA.

_____________________________

item.title: NY school district pauses AI robot teaching assistant rollout amid controversies about manufacturer
item.description: A $60,000 AI humanoid robot named Sally was set to join classrooms, but student data privacy concerns and the company's ties to sex dolls raised alarm.
item.content:encoded:
A school district in rural New York has paused a program to bring in a robot assistant teacher as it reviews privacy concerns.

The Salamanca City Central School District's board initially approved the nearly $60,000 purchase of an AI-driven robot from Realbotix, which would not only be in the classroom, but could communicate with students through their laptops.

The robot, named Sally, is designed to resemble a human, with silicone skin and long brown hair. It will remain seated but will be capable of a range of facial expressions and upper-body movements. The robot would not be a replacement for teachers or staff or operate unsupervised, but be a tutor of sorts that remembers previous interactions with a student and tailors its responses to each student's learning history.

However, the program has met with two major controversies.

WILLIAM BENNETT, JON HAGE: AI CAN MIMIC A TEACHER, BUT IT CANNOT SHEPHERD A SOUL

According to the Associated Press, Realbotix’s sister company, Intima LLC, "holds an ownership stake in RealDoll, a longtime maker of sex dolls, including a line of AI-powered models billed as the ‘world’s most advanced sex robot.’"

Realbotix, however, has asserted that these companies have completely different products with "no crossover."

"Realbotix Corp. is a holding company with two separately operated businesses: Realbotix LLC, which focuses on AI-powered humanoid robotics for commercial service sector applications, and Intima LLC, which focuses on direct-to-consumer products. Realbotix LLC and Intima LLC have different product offerings with no crossover."

The Salamanca City Central School District’s given reason for pausing the program, however, is students’ data concerns regarding any information they share with the robot.

The Associated Press reported that in a now-deleted statement from the district’s Facebook page, the robot teacher assistant pilot program is paused as the district works through "enhanced student data privacy agreements" with the state education officials and does community outreach.

"The robot also has been programmed to steer clear of inappropriate topics such as sex, violence and gambling, and it won’t be able to search the public internet or draw answers from unvetted generative AI services," the Associated Press reported. "Instead, all information on ‘Sally’ will be stored locally, with the life-sized robot consuming roughly the same amount of energy as a laptop, according to the district."

Mark Beehler, Salamanca's superintendent, has addressed concerns about a robot replacing humans in the classroom.

"There is no possible way a robot can replace a human in a school," he said Tuesday. "Even if it were possible, it would in no way be in the best interest of students. Teaching is a human-to-human process."

HUMANOID ROBOT VIDEOS SHOW MACHINES LASHING OUT

He noted, however, that in their rural area, many students do not have easy access to the developing technologies of the future that could help unlock career pathways for them.

"In most cases, our students need to travel 1-2 hours to have opportunities to see emergent technology," he said. "One of the intents of the robot is to help level the playing field and motivate students to continue studying robotics, AI, and STEAM related-career pathways."

When reached by Fox News Digital, the company provided a statement from a Realbotix spokesperson: "Realbotix respects Salamanca City Central School District’s decision to temporarily pause the proposed pilot while the district engages with its community and Realbotix works with the district and the New York State Education Department to put an appropriate data privacy agreement in place. The physical robot has not been deployed."

It provided further clarification on how the robot would protect students’ privacy.

"Realbotix understands the questions being raised by parents and believes they deserve clear, verifiable answers. The proposed physical unit would operate locally through the school and would not be connected to the public internet. It does not record audio or video and does not use facial recognition," the spokesperson said. "Student authentication would be handled entirely through the district’s existing systems, and any student-linked information would remain encrypted and under the district’s control. Realbotix would not receive, access or store personally identifiable student information or student interactions."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

The statement added further that the robot indeed will not be a replacement for teachers , but to "serve as a supervised classroom resource for older high school students participating in the district’s STEAM curriculum. Like a calculator, laboratory apparatus or other instructional tool, it can help students engage with educational material and gain hands-on exposure to AI and robotics, but it does not perform the work of a teacher. Characterizations suggesting that the technology would replace teachers or assume their responsibilities are false."

The company also distanced the robot from any adult associations, arguing that media reports have been outright false.

"Some media reports have also falsely connected the Salamanca project to an adult product or adult-products business. The Salamanca robot is a newly manufactured, purpose-built educational unit; no existing consumer product or hardware is being modified or repurposed for the school. Realbotix LLC focuses exclusively on non-adult commercial applications, including healthcare and education. No adult-products business has any involvement in the Salamanca project or in any product or initiative developed by Realbotix LLC."

Fox News Digital's Rachel del Guidice contributed to this report.

item.title: Foreign robot ban targets China over security fears
item.description: The FCC added foreign-produced humanoid robots and connected power inverters to its Covered List, blocking new models from receiving U.S. authorization.
item.content:encoded:
A humanoid robot can carry equipment through a factory or help researchers test new artificial intelligence. However, its cameras can watch everything nearby. Its internet connection can also send valuable information beyond the building. The Trump administration now sees that combination as a potential national security problem.

On July 28, the Federal Communications Commission added foreign-produced advanced robots and connected power inverters to its Covered List. The action blocks many new models from receiving the FCC authorization required before companies can import or sell them in the United States.

Although the final language applies broadly to foreign-produced equipment, China reportedly sits at the center of the crackdown. Officials want to prevent surveillance and cyberattacks while reducing America's reliance on Chinese technology. They also hope companies will move more manufacturing to the United States.

HUMANOID ROBOT VIDEOS SHOW MACHINES LASHING OUT

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?", has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

Humanoid robots are no longer limited to flashy demonstrations that rack up views online. Companies are preparing them for factories and warehouses. Researchers are also testing them inside laboratories. Four-legged robots can inspect dangerous areas or patrol large properties. Meanwhile, robot developers are building new safety systems as these machines begin working closer to people.

That sounds useful, but these machines also see and hear a lot. Many come equipped with cameras and microphones. Other sensors help them map rooms, recognize objects and respond to people. The robot may connect to cloud services for AI processing. A company might also use that connection to install software updates or provide remote support. That connection is where the FCC sees a potential problem.

If a hacker gets inside the system, the robot could collect sensitive information or send data somewhere it should not go. An attacker might also interfere with its movements. In some cases, that person could gain remote control. We have already seen how those risks can surface in ordinary connected machines. A recent security report involving Yarbo robot mowers raised concerns about remote access, live camera feeds and saved Wi-Fi information.

Now think about a more powerful robot working inside a factory or research lab. Federal national security agencies say some foreign-made robots could create unacceptable cybersecurity and supply chain risks. They worry that hostile governments could use the technology to monitor Americans. The machines could also gather intelligence from sensitive locations. A stolen password is bad enough. A hacked robot can move through a building while recording what it sees. It may also operate close to valuable equipment.

The FCC did not tell Americans to surrender robots they already own. The government also did not automatically order retailers to remove every foreign robot from store shelves. Instead, the agency added foreign-produced advanced robotic devices to its Covered List.

Equipment on that list generally cannot receive a new FCC authorization. Most connected electronic products need that approval before companies can import, market or sell them in the United States. As a result, the restrictions mainly affect new models that have not received authorization. Previously approved products can remain available, although the FCC reportedly retains the authority to revoke earlier approvals.

Companies may also seek conditional approval. Federal national security agencies can review a device and decide whether it presents an acceptable level of risk. Officials expect many non-Chinese suppliers to reportedly receive exemptions. That suggests the broader foreign-made restriction will hit Chinese manufacturers the hardest.

This move did not come out of nowhere. Lawmakers had already introduced a bipartisan proposal that would block federal agencies from using certain robots tied to foreign adversaries. The latest FCC action reaches much further because it can prevent new products from entering the broader American market.

Power inverters rarely attract the same attention as walking robots. Still, they play an important role in America's energy system. An inverter converts direct current electricity into alternating current electricity. Solar panels and batteries generate or store direct current. Homes, power grids and data centers generally need alternating current.

Many inverters today connect to the internet. Operators use those connections to check performance and install updates. Some systems also allow remote adjustments. However, remote access creates another potential doorway for attackers.

Federal officials worry that foreign companies or hackers could interfere with connected inverters. A coordinated attack might disrupt equipment or expose information about how energy moves through a facility.

A major interruption could affect internet cloud services and the businesses that rely on them. An inverter may look like a metal box mounted beside a solar array. Still, when thousands of connected units feed electricity into important systems, their security becomes much harder to ignore.

OHIO ROBOT COP RETIRES AFTER ZERO ARRESTS

Chinese companies have become major players in advanced robotics. They have gained attention by offering capable machines at prices that U.S. developers may struggle to match. The ban could reportedly hit Unitree especially hard. Counterpoint Research estimates that the Chinese company holds just under one-fifth of the global humanoid robot market.

Unitree has also worked with Nvidia to use its Blackwell AI chips in a robot platform. Nvidia has said data from those robots will remain in the United States. The company also said many Unitree customers in America are universities and research institutions. China strongly criticized the FCC action. Its embassy in Washington accused the United States of unfairly targeting Chinese businesses. It also warned that Beijing could respond if the restrictions harm Chinese interests. Meanwhile, China's Foreign Ministry called the policy protectionist. A spokesperson argued that the restrictions could hurt American companies and consumers. We reached out to Unitree for comment, but did not hear back before our deadline.

The foreign robot ban may give U.S. manufacturers more room to grow. American companies will face less competition from low-cost Chinese machines in the domestic market. However, the policy could create short-term problems for researchers and startups. Some American teams use affordable Chinese robots to test software or train AI systems. Losing access to newer models could raise costs and limit the hardware available for experiments.

The restrictions could also complicate partnerships between U.S. chipmakers and Chinese robotics companies. That may slow certain projects even as Washington tries to strengthen domestic production. The bigger question involves timing. Building a competitive American robotics supply chain will take investment and skilled workers. Manufacturers must also secure motors, sensors and other components. Until that happens, tighter restrictions could leave a gap between the robots American developers want and the machines they can afford.

You may never bring a humanoid robot into your home, but smaller connected robots are already everywhere. Robot vacuums, lawn mowers and security devices can collect video, map your property and connect to remote servers. Before you buy one, take a few minutes to check how the company protects that access.

Connected devices sold in the United States should include an FCC identification number. You can usually find it on the product, packaging or manufacturer's website. Be cautious if the company provides no clear regulatory information.

Find out whether the robot stores camera footage and room maps locally or uploads them to the cloud. The privacy policy should explain where the company stores that information and who can access it.

Turn off remote viewing or cloud controls when you do not need them. A feature that lets you control a robot from anywhere could also become an entry point for someone else.

TOP TRUMP AGENCY PURGES OVER 20 SUSPECTED CHINA-LINKED PRODUCTS FROM FEDERAL MARKETPLACE

Robot software needs updates just like your phone or computer. Enable automatic updates when available and avoid products from companies with a poor support record.

Place connected robots and other smart devices on a guest network when your router supports it. That can help keep a compromised device away from your computers and sensitive files.

Use a strong, unique password for the account that controls your robot. A password manager can create and securely store it for you. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) if the manufacturer offers it.

If you are installing a connected solar or battery inverter, ask the installer who can access it remotely. You should also find out how the company handles software updates and what happens if its online service shuts down.

I understand why Washington is paying close attention to this. A network-connected machine with cameras and powerful motors warrants a thorough security review. That concern grows when the robot enters a factory, research center or part of America's energy infrastructure. At the same time, banning new foreign models creates a real tradeoff. Chinese companies currently build many advanced robots at prices American researchers can afford. Restricting that hardware may protect sensitive systems, but it could also slow some U.S. innovation while domestic manufacturers catch up. The success of this policy will depend on what comes next. America needs secure products, strong testing and enough domestic production to give buyers a genuine choice.

Would you accept fewer robot choices and potentially higher prices if the government said the restrictions could prevent foreign surveillance? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: Shark Week advisory as warming seas push blacktips farther north along East Coast
item.description: Blacktip sharks are pushing their summer range as far as Long Island as warming waters reshape migration, putting them closer to swimmers and surfers.
item.content:encoded:
As Shark Week puts the spotlight on ocean predators, researchers say blacktip sharks are spending more time farther north along the East Coast, expanding their summer range into areas where beachgoers historically encountered them less often.

Researchers at Florida Atlantic University say warming ocean temperatures are reshaping the sharks' annual migration, allowing them to travel farther north before returning south for the winter, according to FOX 35 Orlando.

For more than a decade, researchers have tracked blacktip sharks along the East Coast using aerial surveys and satellite tags. Their data shows the sharks travel north each spring, with many reaching as far as Long Island, New York, by late summer, the outlet reported.

SHARK SIGHTINGS SPIKE NEAR AMERICA'S BEACHES AS JULY 4 CROWDS HEAD TO SHORE FOR WEEKEND

As waters continue to warm, researchers expect the sharks to push even farther north while spending less time in South Florida during the winter.

"They are just like us. They like our air-conditioned temperature," Dr. Stephen Kajiura, a Florida Atlantic University professor who has studied blacktip sharks for about 15 years, told FOX 35 Orlando.

"Our room temperature is 72 or so. [That's] the perfect temperature for these blacktip sharks," Kajiura said.

Researchers are already seeing evidence of that shift, with blacktip sharks occurring farther north, including off Long Island, where beachgoers historically encountered the species less frequently, Kajiura noted.

As blacktip sharks swim close to shore, they are among the species beachgoers are most likely to see.

"These are the ones that are in close proximity to the surfers and the swimmers," Kajiura said. "That's the species that's most likely to have encounters with people."

The migration research comes as a new Florida Atlantic University study suggests beach nourishment projects may also influence where blacktip sharks gather during their annual winter migration.

The study, published in the Journal of Coastal Research, found the sharks consistently stay within about 50 meters of the shoreline.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Murky water created by beach nourishment projects could make it harder for the sharks to hunt, potentially changing their behavior and increasing the chances of accidental encounters with people, researchers said.

"What’s striking is how closely the distribution of blacktip sharks overlaps with areas impacted by turbidity events," Kajiura said in a Florida Atlantic University news release.

Researchers said beach nourishment remains an important way to protect coastlines from erosion, but the findings highlight the need to better understand how those projects affect marine life.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Despite the changing migration patterns, Kajiura stressed that shark encounters remain rare and said people shouldn't let the research keep them out of the water.

"The chances of you having a negative encounter with a shark are so minuscule," Kajiura said. "Don't let that diminish your ability to take advantage of the beautiful beaches we have here in Florida."

item.title: Ex-'Squad' member fights for comeback as socialist wing ramps up war on Dem establishment
item.description: Cori Bush's latest campaign ad accuses Wesley Bell of jetting off to Israel with AIPAC instead of helping St. Louis recover from a devastating tornado.
item.content:encoded:
One of the most outspoken members of the "Squad" is plotting her return to Congress as a wave of socialist insurgency continues to batter establishment Democrats across the country.

Former Rep. Cori Bush, D-Mo., is running to get her old seat back representing Missouri's 1st Congressional District after losing to incumbent Rep. Wesley Bell, D-Mo., in November 2024. It's another battle in the wider civil war that's taking place within the Democratic Party.

Missouri's primary elections are this Tuesday, and Bush has spent weeks blasting Bell for his pro-Israel stance and accusing him of being tied too closely to Republicans.

In her latest ad released on Thursday, Bush accused Bell of not doing enough to help St. Louis recover from a May 2025 tornado and instead "jetting off to Israel with AIPAC."

NEW YORK TIMES RAISES EYEBROWS BY REFERRING TO AIPAC AS 'HARD-RIGHT' PRO-ISRAEL GROUP

She posted on X alongside the ad, "When the disaster caused $1.6 billion in damages and took several lives, Wesley responded by hopping on a flight to Israel funded by Trump’s donors less than 90 days later."

Earlier this month, she posted, "Wesley Bell is a former Republican campaign manager who is bought and paid for by AIPAC. On August 4th, we’re going back to DC, and we’ll do it with no corporate cash or AIPAC-funded trips."

BERNIE SANDERS AIMS TO BLOCK SALE OF BOMBS AND BULLDOZERS TO ISRAEL, ACCUSING US ALLY OF 'GENOCIDE'

When reached for comment on Bush's criticism, Bell's campaign pointed Fox News Digital to a recent debate between the two on St. Louis Public Radio, specifically Bell's response to a question on the tornado.

"Once the tornado hit here, I got right to work. I was on the ground immediately, but also working with our delegation, which, you all know, is six Republicans and only myself and [Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, D-Mo.]," Bell said. "And so I got on the phone with each one of them. Sometimes that meant sitting in their offices as well, to explain to them how important it was for them to join me in making certain that St. Louis got the resources that folks here needed. So I'm proud of the fact that we were able to get over $200 million and counting in FEMA disaster relief, but we still got more to do."

Bell's campaign also shared an ad with Fox News Digital in which a constituent called Bush's attacks on Bell "just politics" while defending his response to the tornado.

"Wesley Bell's taken on Trump. He's fighting for me and my neighbors," the constituent said.

The issue of U.S.-Israel relations has been fueling an ever-growing fracture within the Democratic Party since Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on the Jewish nation-state.

The two-term progressive firebrand was one of Congress' harshest critics of Israel and its operation in Gaza, well before it became a more mainstream position in the party. She had accused Israel's government of waging a genocide on Palestinians and consistently voted against emergency funding for the Middle Eastern ally.

BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS

Bell is a more pragmatic Democrat who previously served as a county prosecutor.

Bush blamed her narrow 2024 loss to Bell on hundreds of thousands of dollars spent by pro-Israel groups, including those affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), from outside the district.

The rematch comes as candidates linked to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) continue to shake up primaries across the country.

DSA candidates are posing a challenge for more establishment Democrats in gubernatorial races like Wisconsin and a Senate race in Michigan, and have even successfully toppled House Democratic incumbents in New York and Colorado.

Bush is also a member of the DSA.

item.title: Oregon Ducks tight end reveals unique (and smelly) way quarterback Dante Moore bonds with teammates
item.description: Oregon tight end Jamari Johnson revealed at Big Ten Media Days that Heisman hopeful Dante Moore has a rather gassy habit in the Ducks' huddle.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 college football season is so close you can almost taste it at this point.

As the calendar flips from July to August, teams will start fall camp in the coming days and with that, all the familiar sensory cues will signal that we've nearly made it to the start of another year of football.

The sight of the ball flying through the air, the sound of pads popping in the hot sun, and the smell of freshly cut grass are all reminders of how lucky we are to be alive at a time when college football exists.

ONE OF THESE EIGHT COLLEGE FOOTBALL TEAMS WILL BE HOISTING THE NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP TROPHY IN 2026

Speaking of smells, Oregon tight end Jamari Johnson was at Big Ten Media Days earlier this week, and when asked by KOIN News' Brenna Greene about how quarterback Dante Moore likes to keep things light in the huddle, the rising sophomore revealed some rather stinky information regarding the Ducks' signal caller.

Pardon me?

"Alright guys big fourth down coming up here, we're going hard count so don't false start and also remember, he who smelt it dealt it. Okay, BREAK!"

THREE INTRIGUING QUARTERBACK BATTLES TO WATCH DURING COLLEGE FOOTBALL OFFSEASON CAMPS

Sounds like Moore is channeling his inner Steamin' Willie Beamin and making bodily functions in the huddle cool again.

When it was relayed to Moore that Johnson was speaking out of turn and ruining the sanctity of what happens in the huddle, the Heisman hopeful was less than pleased.

"You gotta find ways to connect with the team, so we do that," said a clearly embarrassed Moore.

MISSOURI'S ELI DRINKWITZ BECOMES LATEST SEC COACH TO MAKE RIDICULOUS COMPLAINTS ABOUT BIG TEN SCHEDULES

He added that "too much stuff is getting leaked out," which is a very poor choice of words on his part, given the context of the conversation.

What's even funnier is that Oregon is historically known for running an up-tempo, no-huddle offense dating all the way back to the Chip Kelly era, and it sounds like head coach Dan Lanning should think about keeping it that way.

If what Johnson says is true, and his players are in the huddle trying to one-up each other in a flatulence competition, it's a miracle they're able to get any of the play calls in on time.

Plus, what if one of those farts turns into something extra? You can't be wasting timeouts for wardrobe changes when you're down three late against Ohio State all because your star quarterback soiled his jock.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

Then again, Oregon finished tied for tenth in the nation with 37 points per game, and Moore is on everyone's short list of Heisman candidates, so maybe stick to what's working.

If it ain't broke, don't fix it.

Go Ducks, fart on!

item.title: Pilot ejects as F-35 crashes at MCAS Miramar, sparking fire
item.description: An F-35 assigned to the 3rd Marine Aircraft Wing crashed Friday morning at MCAS Miramar in San Diego, sparking a brush fire, officials told Fox News.
item.content:encoded:
An F-35B assigned to Marine Aircraft Group 11, 3rd Marine Aircraft Wing, crashed Friday morning on the flight line at Marine Corps Air Station Miramar in San Diego, prompting an emergency response and igniting a brush fire, according to authorities.

Emergency personnel responded to what the Marine Corps described as an "aircraft mishap" on the flight line at about 10 a.m. local time, 1st Lt. Blake Starbuck told Fox News.

According to a Marine Corps news release issued Friday afternoon, the pilot ejected and was taken to a local medical facility in stable condition for evaluation and treatment of injuries that are not life-threatening.

MARINE MISSING FROM USS ANCHORAGE NOW FOCUS OF RECOVERY MISSION OFF CALIFORNIA COAST

The cause of the crash remains under investigation.

Starbuck said he did not immediately have information on the purpose of the flight, whether the aircraft was departing or arriving, or whether it was conducting a training mission. 

The F-35B is the short takeoff and vertical landing variant of the F-35 Lightning II, a fifth-generation stealth fighter built by Lockheed Martin. The aircraft is operated by the Marine Corps and is designed to conduct air-to-air combat, strike missions and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance operations.

LONG-LOST PAN AM CRASH WRECKAGE FOUND DECADES AFTER DEADLY DISASTER THAT RESHAPED AIRLINE SAFETY

Starbuck said he did not immediately have information on the purpose of the flight, whether the aircraft was departing or arriving, or whether it was conducting a training mission.

The Marine Corps routinely investigates aviation mishaps to determine what caused an incident and whether changes are needed to prevent similar accidents. Officials have not said when additional details about the investigation could be released.

Video from SkyRanger 7 showed the aircraft in two pieces amid a football-field-sized scorched area. A fire burned in a field north of State Route 52 and was visible from the freeway, prompting calls to the California Highway Patrol.

The San Diego Fire-Rescue Department confirmed to Fox News it was assisting with the brush fire, but said the military has jurisdiction over the incident. 

Marine Corps Air Station Miramar is home to the 3rd Marine Aircraft Wing, the Marine Corps' principal aviation force on the West Coast. The installation supports a variety of fixed-wing and rotary-wing aircraft used for training and operational missions.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

SOCIALISTS CHEER ‘SHOCKWAVE’ PRIMARY NIGHT AS DSA-BACKED CANDIDATES WIN, ADVANCE ACROSS THE MAP

item.description: Star golfer Charley Hull told critics to "loosen up" after her fake scratch-off ticket prank on caddie Adam Woodward caused a stir on social media.
item.content:encoded:
Golf star Charley Hull pulled off a savage prank on her caddie, Adam Woodward, earlier in the week, and some people were upset about it. She doesn’t care.

Hull, 30, gave Woodward a fake scratch-off lottery ticket, and he thought he had won $100,000. She recounted the tale while speaking with the media ahead of the Women’s British Open at Royal Lytham & St Annes Golf Club in England, and people criticized Hull on social media. Hull had a blunt message for those people.

"No, and people that have complaints about it, I’d say loosen up," Hull told reporters when asked if she regretted it.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

The star golfer said Woodward took it like a champion and thought it was funny.

"He thought it was funny after, he’s not uptight, like it’s a joke. If people don’t like it they can lump it, do you know what I mean? I felt bad for (Woodward) but at the end of the day, I just got to have a good week and then at the end of the week I’ll buy him 100 scratch cards," Hull said.

"Hopefully he can earn more money than that as well this week if we play well."

CHARLEY HULL PULLS OFF SAVAGE LOTTERY PRANK ON HER CADDIE AT WOMEN'S BRITISH OPEN

Hull said she bought the fake scratch-off lottery ticket in town on Monday, and gave it to Woodward on Tuesday. The golfer said Woodward was jubilant after thinking he had struck gold with his newfound fortune.

"He's scratching it, scratching it, scratching, and he's like 'Oh my gosh, I've won' and he's taken his hat off, he's taken his glasses off. He's literally running around the player's lounge saying 'I've won $100,000, I'm taking today off.'

"He was sweating, he was trembling, he couldn't believe his luck, and we had to tell him it was fake and he nearly quit the job," Hull said with a laugh.

Hull has put herself and Woodward in position to make some money at the Women’s Open, as she is tied for seventh at 2-under par after two rounds. She is four strokes off the lead.

item.title: Professional surfer Arran Strong, 28, presumed dead after going missing of the coast of Portugal
item.description: Arran Strong, 28, vanished about a mile off Portugal's coast while crossing between beaches with his coach and is presumed dead after a four-day search.
item.content:encoded:
Professional surfer Arran Strong was presumed dead four days after going missing off the coast of Portugal in a tragic incident, the sports governing body in the UK confirmed.

The 28-year-old was a mile off the coast with his coach, Jose Maria Pyrrait, when the pair stopped to take a drink of water and take pictures. After taking a break for a few minutes, Pyrrait let Strong go ahead of him and then lost sight of him.

"In short: we stopped off Arrifana to drink water and take some pictures. We were there for a few minutes talking, when we started again," Pyrrait wrote in a post on Instagram. "I let him go ahead. Since my pace is faster. I always do that. When I would catch it and get a short lead I’d stop and wait for it."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

"This time it was no different, but when I stopped to wait, I saw your board drifting about 100 meters away. I paddled as fast as I could to get there, diving repeatedly looking for it, but we were in a really deep area and visibility was very short."

Pyrrait said he immediately reached out to his partner on shore for help, and a local fisherman picked him up. They spent nearly 2 1/2 hours "scouring" the area for Strong using the boat’s sonar.

The Autoridade Marítima Nacional (AMN) told BBC Sport it was alerted to Strong having difficulties in the water at 11:33 BST Monday.

"The young man disappeared at sea while crossing from Monte Clerigo Beach to Carrapateira," the AMN told the outlet.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

"His friend, who was with him, was rescued by a local fishing boat that was nearby."

The AMN confirmed that its search for Strong was halted Thursday. Pyrrait said Strong was like a "son" to him in his heartbreaking post.

"Arran was like a son to me; he had been training with me and spending weekends and holidays with me since he was ten years old—as I used to tell his mother, he was like the child of divorced parents. I loved him as if he were another son life had given me," Pyrrait wrote.

"Curiously, he always used to say he would die young. Right now, I feel profound pain; my only faint consolation is that he passed away at sea—a place he loved so dearly. He was young, with a pure and good heart, but he is gone. I feel empty and weary, yet life goes on."

Strong was the highest-ranked British surfer when he competed for Great Britain in each of the last two World Surfing Games. He competed in the World Surf League for a decade.

GB Surfing released a statement on the "tragic passing" of Strong Tuesday.

"Arran proudly represented Great Britain at the 2024 and 2025 ISA World Surf Games, finishing as our highest-placed male surfer on both occasions. Beyond his performances in the water, Arran was a fantastic teammate, respected competitor and a kind, generous presence whose passion for surfing left a lasting impression on everyone who had the privilege of knowing him," the statement said.

"His passing is a devastating loss to our sport and the wider surfing community, and he will be greatly missed. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with Arran’s family, friends, teammates and all those whose lives he touched."

item.title: Brittney Griner files for divorce from wife of 7 years who fought for her release from Russia
item.description: Brittney Griner filed for divorce from Cherelle Griner, who helped get the WNBA star out of a Russian prison, saying the marriage is "irretrievably broken."
item.content:encoded:
WNBA player Brittney Griner has filed for divorce from her wife of seven years, Cherelle, court records show.

Cherelle was a vocal voice during Griner's Russian imprisonment, constantly pleading with U.S. government officials to bring the former Atlanta Dream star home.

When Griner returned home in late 2022, she thanked then-President Joe Biden for his efforts.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

"Over the last 9 months you have been so privy to one of the darkest moments of my life and so today I’m just standing here overwhelmed with emotions but the most important emotion that I have right now is just sincere gratitude for President Biden and his entire administration," Cherelle said with Biden and then-Vice President Kamala Harris by her side.

Cherelle thanked several members of the Biden administration, Griner's former Phoenix Mercury, the WNBPA and Brittney’s agency for doing all they could to keep the WNBA superstar in the spotlight after she was detained, sentenced and then transferred to a Russian penal colony in the final moments of her detention.

"Today, my family is whole. But as you all are aware," Cherelle added. "There are so many other families who are not whole. BG’s not here to say this, but I will gladly speak on her behalf and say that BG and I will remain committed to the work on getting every American home, including Paul (Whelan) whose family is in our hearts today as we celebrate BG being home. We do understand that there’s still people out here who are enduring what I endured the last 9 months of missing, tremendously, their loved ones."

The Griners married in 2019 and share a son, but the WNBA star, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported, said the marriage was "irretrievably broken."

WNBA SUDDENLY WANTS TO STICK TO BASKETBALL AFTER YEARS OF MAKING POLITICS PART OF THE PRODUCT

Griner was freed in a prisoner exchange for convicted Russian arms dealer Viktor Bout. She was arrested at Sheremetyevo Airport in Moscow on Feb. 17, 2022, after Russian authorities said she had vape cartridges with cannabis oil inside her luggage. On Aug. 4 of that year, Griner was given a nine-year sentence after pleading guilty, arguing that she had been prescribed cannabis for her pain and inadvertently packed it. Her sentence was upheld in October, and she was later transferred to a penal colony.

Bout is known as the "Merchant of Death" and the possible swap for him was floated back in May. He was in the middle of a 25-year sentence in federal prison after he was convicted of conspiracy to kill Americans relating to the support of a Colombian terrorist organization.

Griner wrote in her memoir that she expected Cherelle to get a divorce if she had actually stayed in Russia for her entire prison sentence.

"My basketball career would be over. I’d be in my early forties and out of shape, would have to find a new way to provide for my wife. And Relle. She assured me she’d wait, but ten years was ridiculous," Griner wrote, via Complex.

"I went through so many emotions being locked up, and just thinking about nine years," she continued. "We planned on having kids, and doing all these amazing things together, and now I'm thinking, ‘Is that going to happen? How can I ask her to wait?’"

This would be Griner's second divorce. Griner married then-fellow WNBA star Glory Johnson in May 2015, despite both being arrested on charges of domestic violence against one another just three weeks prior. Johnson announced the following months she was pregnant via IVF and a sperm donor, and Griner filed for divorce the next day. That divorce was finalized June 2016.

Griner filed for the divorce on Thursday, and a hearing is slated for Sept. 1. She now plays for the Connecticut Sun.

Fox News' Ryan Gaydos contributed to this report.

item.title: American Red Cross declares national blood crisis as type O supply drops to dangerous levels
item.description: The American Red Cross declared a blood crisis across the nation as donations hit a four-year summer low, forcing limits on type O blood distributions to hospitals.
item.content:encoded:
The American Red Cross has declared a "blood crisis" across the nation.

The organization released a warning about the second-ever blood supply crisis this week after blood donations fell to a four-year summer low.

This decline worsens an emergency shortage that "threatens the availability of lifesaving blood for patients across the country," the organization wrote in a press release.

MICROPLASTICS DETECTED IN MOST HEART ATTACK PATIENTS' BLOOD IN STARTLING NEW STUDY

The Red Cross is now limiting distributions of type O blood to hospitals, as the nation’s largest single provider of blood products now has less than a one-day national supply of type O positive blood.

Type O blood accounts for about 60% of Red Cross blood distributions and is essential for both everyday patient care and medical emergencies.

Type O positive is the most commonly transfused blood type, according to the Red Cross, and can be safely given to about 80% of patients. 

Type O negative remains the universal blood type "relied upon when every second counts."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

While thousands of Americans show up to donate blood, these donations are reportedly not keeping up with hospital demand during summer trauma season.

This summer’s conditions, amid extreme heat, poor air quality and foodborne illnesses, have contributed to lower donor turnout, the Red Cross reported. Other blood collectors have also reported critical shortages this summer.

The Red Cross advised that just three more donors at each blood drive can end the crisis and stabilize the blood supply.

It encourages Americans to book an appointment by using the Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood.org, or by calling 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733-2767).

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Chris Hrouda, president of Red Cross Biomedical Services, shared information about the developing emergency in a statement.

"The Red Cross takes its responsibility as the nation’s largest single provider of blood products incredibly seriously and has worked tirelessly to strengthen the blood supply for our hospital partners," he said.

Following the organization’s first national blood crisis in January 2022, Hrouda said the Red Cross has put "additional safeguards" in place to help "prevent a crisis like that from happening again."

"But this summer, blood donations simply are not keeping pace with hospital demand, and inventories — especially type O blood — remain under significant strain," he said.

"Every donation has the potential to help save lives, and we urgently need everyone who is eligible to make an appointment to give blood as soon as possible."

item.title: Washington Post opinion editor to exit paper after just one year, staff completely 'blindsided'
item.description: A source says Post leadership was "blindsided" by Adam O'Neal's exit after he reshaped the opinion section to champion free markets and liberties.
item.content:encoded:
Washington Post opinion editor Adam O'Neal announced his exit from the paper on Friday after roughly just one year on the job.

"I’m writing to announce that I have decided to leave The Washington Post. My last day will be August 31," O'Neal told staff in a memo obtained by Fox News Digital.

"I joined The Post to lead the opinion section as it began a new chapter, and we have made dramatic changes over the past year. We quickly embraced our mission of championing free markets and personal liberties while simultaneously putting Post Opinions on a sustainable footing. Our work has become more relevant, accessible and consequential. We regularly publish world-class journalism that finds the audience where it is," O'Neal wrote before touting improvements in the opinion section's page views and time spent on the site.

EDITORIAL OVERHAUL: WASHINGTON POST'S NEW OPINION CHIEF FEELS THE WEIGHT OF THE CHALLENGES AHEAD

"I want to thank Jeff Bezos, Jeff D’Onofrio and the entire leadership team. And I especially want to thank everyone in Post Opinions. It has been an honor to have worked with such exceptional people at such an exceptional institution. While this was not an easy decision, I am leaving proud of how far the opinion section has come and optimistic that its best days lie ahead," he added.

Jeff D’Onofrio, The Washington Post's acting CEO and publisher, thanked O'Neal and crediting him for making the opinion section "more balanced in perspective, more financially sustainable and more accessible to readers than ever before," adding that a leadership transition will be in the works leading up to his Aug. 31 departure.

JEFF BEZOS REPORTEDLY TOLD TRUMP THE WASHINGTON POST WAS HIS ‘WORST INVESTMENT’ BEFORE STAFF CUTS

A source familiar with O'Neal's exit told Fox News Digital that Post leadership was "blindsided" by the decision and there were no tensions between him and D’Onofrio and owner Jeff Bezos.

O'Neal held an all-hands meeting with staff where he revealed it was a "personal decision" to leave The Post and that everyone in the room was "incredibly surprised," according to a staffer who attended the meeting.

O'Neal did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

JEFF BEZOS' TENURE AS WASHINGTON POST OWNER IN SPOTLIGHT AS PAPER GRAPPLES WITH LOW MORALE, STAFFER EXODUS 

O'Neal joined The Post last July after serving as a correspondent for the British outlet The Economist and as an editorial page writer for The Wall Street Journal. He was tasked to carry out Bezos' directive that The Post's editorial pages would promote "personal liberties and free markets," something that sparked intense backlash among both staffers in the newsroom and liberal critics. 

Bezos' edict led to the immediate resignation of O'Neal's predecessor, David Shipley. 

In his first interview as The Post opinion editor, O'Neal told Fox News Digital in September he felt "a tremendous responsibility to get this right."

"Our readers are overwhelmingly liberal, right?" O'Neal conceded. "And they're all overwhelmingly located in blue states. And just a few blue states. And they're over-represented on the coasts. And so, one way to look at it would be to say, 'Well, if you're non-partisan, and you have a highly partisan readership, they may be offended by that.' And maybe that's true. But looking forward as I rebuild, I really just see it as an opportunity to expand our reach."

He continued, "And frankly, a lot of people don't trust The Post. And they don't trust the mainstream media more broadly. And so my mission is to hire the kinds of people from throughout the U.S. with different kinds of backgrounds, intellectual diversity, who can appeal and rebuild that trust. And I think that a lot of folks have a poor view of The Post because they don't feel that they've been well served by it."

item.title: Michigan hospital pays $410K to settle lawsuit by physician assistant fired over transgender policy
item.description: Valerie Kloosterman says she was fired three weeks after requesting a religious accommodation from mandatory gender identity training at the hospital.
item.content:encoded:
A Michigan hospital has agreed to pay $410,000 to settle a lawsuit brought by a physician assistant who said she was fired after refusing to comply, due to her faith convictions, with workplace policies related to transgender patients, according to court filings and statements from the parties.

Valerie Kloosterman sued University of Michigan Health-West after she was terminated in August 2021.

"All I wanted to do was provide the best care possible to my patients without being forced to violate my Christian beliefs," Kloosterman said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.

CHRISTIAN SCHOOL CHAPLAIN WINS SETTLEMENT AFTER FIRING OVER LGBTQ SERMON

First Liberty Institute, which represents Kloosterman, said she had received positive performance reviews throughout her employment before raising faith-based objections to mandatory gender identity training.

The organization told Fox News Digital Kloosterman was fired three weeks after requesting a religious accommodation from finishing a mandatory training that required her to affirm statements about gender identity that were in violation of her Christian faith.

According to First Liberty Institute, UMHW made no effort to accommodate her beliefs. She sued in October 2022.

CHRISTIAN LIFEGUARD WHO REFUSED PRIDE FLAG DUTIES AND WAS SUSPENDED IS NOW HEADED TOWARD TRIAL

The lawsuit says University of Michigan Health-West officials called her to a meeting, where they disparaged her religious beliefs, called her "evil" and a "liar," told her she could not bring her Christian beliefs into the workplace, and accused her of contributing to suicides among individuals with gender dysphoria.

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

The settlement, according to the legal group, calls for UMHW to make a religious accommodation policy that complies with the law, inform and train all employees, give reasonable religious accommodations without retribution to those who request it, and pay the $410,000 in damages and fees to Ms. Kloosterman and her attorneys.

"This new policy ensures that providers of faith and employees at UMHW will receive religious accommodations so that they can provide excellent care consistent with their medical judgment, because all patients are created in the image of God," Kloosterman said in her statement to Fox News Digital.

GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS

"Title VII prohibits employers from discriminating against and punishing employees for their faith," Kayla Toney, counsel at First Liberty, said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital. "Valerie is an exceptional physician assistant who cares for each of her patients. Employers cannot drive out people like Valerie just because of their sincere religious beliefs. We are grateful to have resolved this matter with University of Michigan Health-West."

Fox News Digital reached out to University of Michigan Health-West for comment.

item.title: Fauci faces lifetime ban from federal government work under new bill following explosive hearing
item.description: Rep. Rich McCormick's bill could ban Anthony Fauci from federal employment after he invoked the Fifth Amendment over 100 times before Rand Paul.
item.content:encoded:
A House GOP proposal would bar Dr. Anthony Fauci from working for the federal government again after his dramatic hearing on Capitol Hill this week.

Fauci appeared before the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, chaired by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., where he invoked the Fifth Amendment over 100 times.

Republicans have been hammering the former public health official over the move, and now a new bill by Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga., would bar him from returning to his old duties and potentially open him to criminal prosecution.

RAND PAUL SEEKS CONTEMPT CHARGES AFTER FAUCI INVOKES FIFTH AMENDMENT MORE THAN 100 TIMES

"We saw him evade so many questions, pleading the Fifth... that's fine, that's your constitutional right," McCormick said in a video shared with Fox News Digital. "But you also have the right, if your till comes up short at Burger King, when your boss asks you why are you short $20 in your cash register — if you plead the Fifth, that's your... ability, but I can fire you."

He argued, "It should be the same way in government. If you don't want to answer questions about what you did wrong, we should be able to fire you."

The bill, called the STOP the SWAMP Act, would bar people from working for the federal government if they refuse to answer certain questions from federal lawmakers or if they are convicted of perjury, according to a news release on McCormick's website.

EXCLUSIVE: BIDEN PARDON WON'T SHIELD FAUCI IF HE LIES TO CONGRESS, COMER SAYS

It would also authorize members of Congress to refer hearing witnesses for prosecution if they were found to have unlawfully withheld information from lawmakers, the release said.

Fauci is not currently facing any criminal charges and has consistently denied any wrongdoing. But Paul, a longtime critic of Fauci's, said his committee would begin the process for holding the doctor in contempt of Congress after the hearing.

Fauci appeared before the Senate GOP-led panel on Wednesday amid new scrutiny over how he handled the COVID-19 pandemic, following the release of a diary he kept during the global health crisis.

FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

Diary entries made public by Paul ahead of the hearing showed the high-profile doctor reflecting on his pandemic-era fame and discussing the disease's origins.

Some entries appeared to show Fauci taking credit for influencing policies that closed schools during the pandemic, one of the most hotly debated aspects of how the government handled COVID.

He told the House Oversight Committee in January 2024, however, "I did not close the schools."

The longtime doctor became the public face of the U.S. government's COVID-19 response and drew both praise and criticism.

He previously served as director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases from 1984 to 2022.

item.title: Top Wisconsin Democratic socialist candidate confronted on past 'defund police' rhetoric
item.description: Francesca Hong confirmed her DSA membership since 2020 but says her views on police abolition have evolved since her earlier social media posts.
item.content:encoded:
Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial frontrunner Francesca Hong defended her active membership in the Democratic Socialists of America while attempting to distance herself from some of its most extreme proposals Friday.

Speaking on "America’s Newsroom," Hong was confronted over previous posts endorsing far-left causes like abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), dismantling the Senate and defunding the police. Her appearance came a month after she appeared on Hasan Piker’s broadcast, where she defended many of the DSA’s policies.

Fox News’ Dana Perino questioned whether there was anything Hong disagreed with regarding the DSA platform, to which she responded that abolishing the Senate is "nonsensical and non-practical at this time." She also rejected their platform of getting rid of the Supreme Court, citing a belief in checks and balances.

DEMOCRATIC WISCONSIN GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE DOESN'T RECALL 'ABOLISH THE SENATE' POST IN 2021, CAMPAIGN SAYS

Perino then asked directly whether Hong was personally a dues-paying member of the socialist organization.

"In my home chapter in Madison, I have been since 2020," Hong confirmed, describing herself as a "democratic socialist," "a good single mom" and a "service industry worker."

However, Perino pressed Hong on past social media posts where she repeatedly called for police abolition, asking: "Why shouldn't people take you at your word when you say that you want to defund the police and go towards abolishing it?"

WISCONSIN DEM SOCIALIST GUBERNATORIAL HOPEFUL DODGES WHETHER SHE STILL WANTS TO ‘ABOLISH POLICE’

Hong said her views had evolved, replying, "I believe that people can evolve. We meet Trump voters from previous elections who now would like to vote for me."

"So who needs to evolve, the voter or you?" Perino asked. Hong then rejected her previous position, noting that the governor of Wisconsin would be unable to defund the police, and promising that if elected she "won’t defund the police."

The focus on the DSA’s platform has highlighted a rift in the Democratic Party, as many moderate Democrats reject its policies, despite several DSA candidates notching primary wins, including in New York and Colorado.

In June, Hong appeared on Piker’s stream, where she confirmed aspects of her platform, including supporting universal childcare, free school meals, abolishing ICE, public grocery stores and legalizing cannabis, among others.

Polling has Hong poised to take the Democratic nomination for Wisconsin governor, despite frequently being pressed by outlets about her past statements online. She has been backed by local Wisconsin DSA chapters and has gotten public support from key Democratic figures, including Reps. Ilhan Omar and Ro Khanna.

FORMER CLINTON OFFICIAL WARNS 'RADICAL' SOCIALIST TAKEOVER WILL 'DESTROY' THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY IF UNCHECKED

Hong called for abolishing police in a 2021 social media post after federal prosecutors chose not to charge the officer accused of shooting Jacob Blake, a Black man, in Kenosha. She addressed those comments in a May statement to Fox News Digital but did not say then whether she continued to support abolishing the police.

"There is no way I want to cut resources for public safety," Hong said. "I don’t like crime. I don’t like unsafe streets. I also don’t like when a member of law enforcement abuses their power."

Her campaign also previously addressed her "Abolish the Senate" comments, noting she did not recall making the post in 2021, which came after the Senate failed to convict President Donald Trump during impeachment proceedings.
